I’m 71 years old, and I’ve been farming these 3 mu in Quzhou County for half a century. My son and his wife work off‑farm at a factory in Handan, so it’s mostly me and my wife in the fields, though they come back to help at harvest. I know this soil and this climate better than any book. I don’t try fancy new tricks anymore—I stick to what works, saves labor, and doesn’t wear me out.

For the **winter wheat**, I sowed it last October with improved Jimai seed from the county supply cooperative. Now that it’s returning green, I will topdress urea at the jointing stage and irrigate three times: once now to wake it up after winter, once at booting, and once at grain filling if the sky stays dry. I’ll spray herbicide once and a fungicide once if I see any rust spots. I always run the rotary tiller before wheat sowing to get a fine seedbed.

For the **summer maize**, as soon as the wheat comes off in early June I will plant hybrid seed straight into the wheat stubble without plowing—there’s no time to waste between crops, and my back isn’t what it used to be. I’ll put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea at the big‑trumpet stage. I’ll irrigate twice, at jointing/booting and grain filling, depending on the rain. One pesticide spray is usually enough unless the armyworms show up.

I don’t chase record yields anymore. I aim for steady, decent harvests with moderate inputs, because at my age the most important thing is to farm sustainably without exhausting myself or spending money I don’t need to.
